originalRecord.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.

originalRecord.q: Refer to the fireworks graph. At four shared displays, an analyst records only North’s marginal benefit and recommends reducing provision because it is below MC. What corrects this recommendation?
options: Add South’s $20,000 to North’s $30,000; the fourth shared display meets the $50,000 marginal cost.
Add the neighborhoods’ quantities to obtain eight displays and compare that with MC.
Use only North’s $30,000 because the larger valuation replaces the smaller one.
Average the two valuations to obtain $25,000 and reduce provision.
originalRecord.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
originalRecord.feedback: Both neighborhoods consume the same four displays. The marginal values add vertically: 30,000 + 20,000 = $50,000, equal to MC. Neither a quantity sum nor an average values the shared marginal display correctly.

originalRecord.q: Use the Lorenz curve. If total income is $200 million, how much goes to the bottom 60%, and why would assigning them $120 million misread the graph?
options: $120 million; the equality line gives the observed income distribution.
$140 million; subtract their 30% income share from 100%.
$60 million; 60% is their population share, while their income share is 30%.
$30 million; treat the percentage income share as a dollar amount.
originalRecord.feedback: The curve assigns 30% of income to the bottom 60% of people. 0.30×$200 million=$60 million; equal population shares do not imply equal income shares.
originalRecord.imageAlt: Lorenz curve showing the bottom 40 percent receiving 15 percent of income.
originalRecord.graphDescription: The equality line is diagonal. The Lorenz curve passes through cumulative population-income points (20,5), (40,15), (60,30), (80,55), and (100,100); the bottom-40-percent reading is highlighted.
originalRecord.graphScenario: single Lorenz curve with quintile readings

afterRecord.q: Total income is $200 million. Using the Lorenz curve, how much goes to the bottom 60%, and why is applying their population percentage directly to income incorrect?
options: $80 million; population share differs from the plotted income share.
$60 million; a population share is always the same as an income share.
$60 million; population share differs from the plotted income share.
$80 million; a population share is always the same as an income share.
afterRecord.feedback: At population 60%, the curve gives income share 30%. Thus the group receives 0.30 × 200 = $60 million. $120 million would use the equality benchmark instead of the observed distribution.
